title: Restraint and Restrictive Practice Policy
summary: Our policy on restraint and restrictive practice in people's homes: what counts as restraint and restriction, the practices our staff never use, the only restrictions we allow and how each is consented to or decided in the person's best interests, approved, recorded, reviewed and reduced, how we prevent distress, medicines used to manage behaviour, and what happens after any emergency intervention. For all employees.

keyPoints.intro: Restraint and restrictions take away a person's freedom. This tells you what you must never do, what you may do only when the care plan approves it, and what to do if someone is about to be seriously hurt.
points: Never hold, pin, restrain or force anyone to accept care, medicines, food or a move. If the person resists, stop, try the care plan's other approaches later in the visit, and phone the office before you leave if an essential task is not done.

Use only the restrictions the care plan records as approved, exactly as the visit plan says. Never add one yourself or agree to a relative's request to lock a door, take keys or stop someone going out.
Never take away or move out of reach a walking aid, wheelchair, phone, alarm, glasses or hearing aid, or use a bed rail, furniture or bedding to stop someone getting up.
Never withhold food, drink, cigarettes, money, outings or contact as a punishment or reward, never threaten or trick anyone, and never shut anyone in a room.

Leave the door openable from inside unless the person chooses otherwise or the care plan records an approved restriction. If someone who cannot keep safe outside walks out, go with them and keep them in sight without holding or blocking them, and phone the office.

Before you raise bed rails or fasten a lap belt, check they fit as the plan says. If the person objects, tries to climb out or gets a limb trapped, do not use it and phone the office before you leave.
Know each person's triggers and what helps. Slow down, give space and choices, try again later in the visit, and if you feel unsafe leave at once and phone the office.
Only if someone is about to be seriously hurt and nothing else will work in time may you act physically, such as moving a hand from a lit hob, with the least force for the shortest time.
Afterwards, stay with the person, check for injuries, call 999 if needed, and phone the office before you leave. Report it in the CareFlow app as a safeguarding incident before your shift ends.
Give a when required medicine for distress only as its guidance says, after trying the other approaches first, and phone the office before you leave.

Phone the office before you leave if anyone, including a colleague, restrains the person, locks them in or keeps people away, or the person seems over-sedated. Report the same day any objection to a restriction.
Complete restrictive practice awareness at induction before working without a shadowing colleague, then every 12 months, and person-specific training before you use any restriction.

blocks.p: {{organisation}} supports people in their own homes, where they have the right to come and go, to move freely, to keep their belongings and to live as they choose. Restraint and restrictions take those freedoms away, can cause physical and emotional harm, and can be abuse. We are committed to the least restrictive practice and to the human rights of every person we support.

{{organisation}} does not use planned physical restraint and does not train staff in holding or restraint. The only physical action our staff may ever take is an emergency intervention to stop someone being seriously hurt when nothing else would work in time. Any other restriction, such as bed rails, a lap belt, a door sensor or locked storage, is used only when it is necessary, proportionate, the least restrictive option and a last resort, agreed by the person or decided in their best interests, and approved by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager. Every restriction is recorded, reviewed and reduced or ended as soon as it can be.

This policy sets out how we meet Regulation 13 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and the Human Rights Act 1998 in home care, following the Department of Health's Positive and Proactive Care guidance, so that distress is prevented, prohibited practices are never used, every restriction is lawful, approved, reviewed and reduced, and every emergency intervention is learned from.

This policy applies to the Directors, the Nominated Individual, managers, office and care staff, bank and agency workers, students and volunteers. It covers every adult we support, however funded and whether or not they have capacity, and any restriction our staff use, monitor or are asked to apply, including those proposed by relatives or other professionals.

This policy does not repeat: capacity assessment and best interests decisions (Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy); signed consent and verifying attorneys and deputies (Consent to Care Policy); possible deprivation of liberty (Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure); staff safety, behaviour and aggression risk assessments and breakaway training (Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy); bed rail checks (Hoists, Slings and Lifting Equipment Procedure); covert medicines (Covert Administration of Medicines Policy); when required medicines guidance (When Required (PRN) Medicines Protocol); choosing sensors and devices (Technology-Enabled Care and Telecare Policy); and a missing person (No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure).

rows: Restraint

Using or threatening force to make a person do something they resist, or restricting their liberty of movement whether or not they resist, including by physical, mechanical or chemical means (Regulation 13(7); Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 6(4)).
Restriction
Any limit on what a person may do or where they may go, including restraint, and any limit on their access to belongings, food, money or people, or on their privacy.
Significant restriction

Our term, from the Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure, for any of these, by anyone: being locked in or kept from going out; being stopped or brought back when trying to leave; supervision or monitoring for all or most of the day and night; physical restraint or being held for care; covert medicines or medicines to sedate or control behaviour; limits on seeing people or using the phone. Where the person lacks or may lack capacity, it is always referred.
Restrictive practice

Any restriction, and any practice, equipment, medicine or arrangement that has the effect of restricting a person, whether or not that is its purpose. It may be physical, mechanical (such as bed rails, lap belts or tightly tucked bedding), chemical (medicines to calm or sedate), environmental (such as locked doors or cupboards or an isolated cooker), technological (monitoring devices) or psychological.
Emergency intervention

A brief, unplanned physical action by our staff to stop immediate serious harm to the person or someone else when nothing less restrictive would work in time. It is always reported as unapproved restraint.
Supportive touch
Touch the person accepts, such as holding an offered hand, a hand on the back to guide them to a chair or moving and handling under their plan. It becomes restraint the moment the person resists.
Monitoring device

Any door, bed, chair or room sensor, activity monitor, tracker, camera, audio monitor, or alarm set to alert when the person gets up, leaves a room or goes out. It is always a restriction. A safety alarm that alerts only when pressed or on a detected emergency (pendant, pull cord, worn fall detector, seizure alarm, linked smoke, heat or carbon monoxide detectors) is not, nor is a camera used only for home security.
Blanket restriction
A rule applied to a person or household for convenience or habit rather than because of an assessed individual risk, such as all knives locked away when only one person is at risk.
Approved restriction

A restriction with a recorded legal basis (signed consent, an approved best interests decision, a verified attorney's or deputy's decision, or a Court of Protection order) and approved in CareFlow under this policy.

blocks.p: The Directors are accountable for {{organisation}} meeting Regulation 13 and approve this policy. The Nominated Individual is the board-level lead for reducing restrictive practice: they challenge the restrictive practice figures in the quarterly quality report, receive the annual restrictive practice report and make sure the Directors agree its reduction actions.

The Registered Manager is the restrictive practice lead. They approve restrictions, keep the restrictive practice register, review it monthly, lead post-incident reviews of emergency interventions and report to the Nominated Individual. The Deputy Manager also approves restrictions, does the monthly audit and covers these duties in the Registered Manager's absence. Covert medicines are approved only by the Registered Manager or, during an absence, an acting manager whose appointment letter gives that authority (Covert Administration of Medicines Policy).

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators and Field Care Supervisors

blocks.p: As authorised assessors they identify, assess and review restrictions, obtain signed consent or prepare best interests decisions, and write what staff do and must never do into the visit plans. Care Coordinators check review dates weekly, tell commissioners, arrange person-specific training and brief care workers.

Out of hours, the On-call Manager receives reports of emergency interventions and restrictions by others, acts as the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure requires, obtains phone approval from the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager before any new restriction is used, records who approved it and when, and hands over by 10am on the next working day.

subsections.heading: Senior Care Workers and Care Workers

blocks.p: They follow the care plan's approaches to prevent distress, use only approved restrictions exactly as recorded, never use a prohibited practice, and report as the key points set out. Senior Care Workers check that colleagues do the same at visits they share, and show new workers each person's approved restrictions on shadowing shifts.

The HR Manager keeps training records current and makes sure no worker is allocated to apply a restriction they are not trained in. Office staff record every report about a restriction in the daily visit notes, pass it to the Care Coordinator the same working day, and put any report of restraint, an emergency intervention or a restriction by others straight through to the safeguarding lead (the On-call Manager out of hours).

bullets: Regulation 13(4)(b) forbids care that includes acts intended to control or restrain a person that are not necessary to prevent, or not a proportionate response to, a risk of harm to the person or another individual. Regulation 13(5) forbids depriving a person of their liberty for care without lawful authority, which at home only the Court of Protection can give (Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure).

Under sections 5 and 6 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, an act intended to restrain a person is protected only where the person doing it reasonably believes that the person lacks capacity for the matter and that the act is necessary to prevent harm to them, and the act is proportionate to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. Restraining a person who has capacity against their will is unlawful, apart from reasonable force in self-defence, to protect another person or to prevent a crime (Criminal Law Act 1967, section 3).

The Human Rights Act 1998 protects the right not to be subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment (Article 3), the right to liberty (Article 5), respect for private and family life and home (Article 8) and freedom from discrimination in those rights (Article 14). Under section 73 of the Care Act 2014 we are treated as exercising a public function, and must act compatibly with these rights, when providing care that a local authority arranges or pays for, wholly or partly, under that Act. Our policy is to apply the same standard to everyone we support, however their care is funded.

CQC guidance on Regulation 13 expects zero tolerance of abuse, unlawful discrimination and restraint, training so that control, restraint and restrictive practices are used only when absolutely necessary and as a last resort, and regular monitoring and review of their use.

blocks.p: Our policy is stricter than the law. We follow the Positive and Proactive Care key actions that apply to home care: no restraint affecting breathing or circulation, no deliberate pain, no seclusion, the least restrictive option for the immediate need, people and families involved in every plan, and behaviour support plans for people at risk of restrictive practice.

Every decision about a restriction takes account of the person's disability, culture, religion, age, sex and communication needs, never rests on a diagnosis, age or behaviour alone, and is explained to them and their family in the format they need (Communication and Accessible Information Policy).

Using any of these is a safeguarding concern and a disciplinary matter, whoever asked for it and whatever the reason. Anyone who sees a colleague use one, or any restriction that is not approved, phones the office before leaving the visit, and it is logged in the incident log the same day.

bullets: planned physical restraint or holding of any kind, including holding a person still for personal care, oral care, medicines, dressing or moving and handling;

any hold or position that could affect breathing or circulation, such as face down on any surface, pressure on the chest, neck, back or abdomen, or sitting or lying on a person, and any technique that causes pain;

shutting a person in a room, or locking a person alone in their home so that they cannot get out, unless a Court of Protection order expressly authorises it and the Registered Manager has approved the fire safety arrangements after a home fire safety visit by the fire and rescue service;
removing or putting out of reach a walking aid, wheelchair, phone, call alarm, glasses, hearing aids or communication aid;

using bed rails, chairs, tables, furniture or bedding to stop a person getting up or leaving their bed or chair, or a lap belt or harness for any purpose other than the posture or safety need it was prescribed or assessed for;
giving any medicine to sedate or control a person without the prescriber's written decision, giving a medicine by force or against a refusal, or giving it covertly without an approved plan;
withholding food, drink, cigarettes, money, outings, activities or contact with others as a punishment, a reward or to control behaviour;
threats, intimidation, humiliation or deception to make a person do something, including saying a relative or the doctor insists;
blanket restrictions, and any restriction a relative, friend or other professional asks our staff to apply that has not been approved under this policy.

blocks.p: Care workers never take or hide a person's keys, and leave the door so the person can open it from inside, unless the person chooses otherwise or an approved restriction says otherwise. A person who wants to go out is never stopped: the care worker follows the visit plan and phones the office before leaving. If the person cannot keep safe outside alone and walks out during a visit, the care worker goes with them, keeps them in sight and encourages them back without holding or blocking them, phones the office, and phones 999 if they lose sight of them, under the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure.
Distress is usually how a person shows fear, pain or an unmet need. We reduce it by knowing the person well, so that restriction is rarely considered.

bullets: At assessment and every care plan review, the assessor asks the person and those who know them what triggers distress, its early signs, what helps and what makes it worse, and about any restraint or restriction used in the past or by others. The Care Coordinator obtains any behaviour support plan, as the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy sets out.

My needs and support and the visit plans record the person's routines, how to communicate with them, early signs of distress, the approaches to use and in what order, what to avoid, when to stop and try later, and who to phone. A specialist behaviour support plan is followed in full and its key points are copied into the care plan.

Care workers look first for a cause: pain, infection, constipation, hunger, thirst, needing the toilet, poor sleep, hearing or sight problems, a medicine change, noise, being rushed or an unfamiliar care worker. New, sudden or worse distress is phoned to the office before the care worker leaves, and the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) contacts the GP the same day.

If distress rises during a visit, the care worker stops the task, gives space and choices and tries again later in the visit; if they feel unsafe they leave at once, even with care unfinished, and phone the office (Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy).

Care Coordinators keep a consistent team and unhurried visits for people who become distressed, ask the commissioner in writing within 2 working days for more time or support where it would avoid a restriction, and request specialist advice within the timescales in the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy.

sections.heading: Assessing, agreeing and approving a restriction

blocks.p: A restriction may be proposed by the person, a relative, a health professional, a commissioner or our own staff, or found in place at assessment, including one used in hospital before a discharge. Care workers never start a restriction themselves. Whoever receives a proposal tells the Care Coordinator the same working day. The Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) records it in the care plan and updates the deprivation of liberty screen the same working day, and the Care Coordinator arranges a restrictive practice assessment as a focused review within 7 days under the Care Plan Review Procedure. For a planned package, restrictions are assessed and approved before the first visit.

At a short-notice start, or where the person would be at risk before the assessment is complete, the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager may approve an interim restriction by phone until then, recorded in the care plan with the reasons. It needs the signed consent of a person with capacity. Where the person cannot decide and has no formal capacity assessment yet, it is a best interests decision for one visit at a time under the Consent to Care Policy, renewed by phone for each visit until the formal capacity assessment and best interests decision are complete. While waiting for a decision during a visit, the care worker does not use the restriction, gives the care the person agrees to, makes them as safe as possible without it, and waits up to 30 minutes after the planned end of the visit (the On-call Manager answers or returns calls within 15 minutes); after that the office arranges an extra visit.

An authorised assessor completes the assessment with the person, at their best time and with the communication help they need, and records it in the risk assessments and the Consent and decisions part of the care plan:

steps: Record the risk the restriction would address, with evidence from incidents and daily visit notes, rated by the method in the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure, and the causes and triggers found and what has been done about them.
Record every less restrictive option, including doing nothing, which have been tried, for how long, and why they did not work or are not suitable.
Record exactly what the restriction is, when and by whom it is used, how long it lasts, what staff must check each time, and what staff must never do.

Record the person's own views, in their words where possible, and the views of the people they want involved and of relevant professionals, such as an occupational therapist for bed rails or lap belts.
Record the possible harms of the restriction to the person, physical and emotional, and how they will be watched for.
Set a review date and a reduction goal: what would need to change for the restriction to be reduced or ended.

rows: Has capacity and agrees

Signed consent under the Consent to Care Policy, obtained after the assessor has spoken with the person alone to check they are not under pressure; then Registered Manager or Deputy Manager approval. The person may withdraw consent at any time, and the restriction stops at once.
Has capacity and does not agree
The restriction is not used. Risks the person chooses to take are managed under the Positive Risk-Taking Policy.
Lacks capacity for the decision about the restriction

A formal capacity assessment and a best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy, approved by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager before use (covert medicines only by the Registered Manager or an authorised acting manager), with a best interests meeting within 10 working days and, where only paid staff can be consulted, the Care Coordinator asks the local authority in writing within 2 working days to consider an IMCA. A verified health and welfare attorney or deputy with authority for the decision decides instead; we still assess and approve our part in the restriction, we do not apply a restriction they refuse, and the Registered Manager writes to the local authority within 2 working days about any decision of theirs that seems not to be in the person's best interests.
Covered by a Court of Protection order
Only the measures the order authorises, used as the Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure sets out, and still only where needed.

blocks.p: The approver checks that the restriction is necessary, proportionate, the least restrictive option and not a blanket restriction, that the deprivation of liberty screen has been decided, and that every allocated care worker has had any person-specific training. Nobody approves an assessment they prepared. Out of hours, approval is given by phone through the On-call Manager, and the approver confirms it in CareFlow by the end of the next working day.

bullets: The Care Coordinator writes the restriction into the visit plans, tells every rostered care worker before their next visit and tells the commissioner in writing within 2 working days of each new or changed restriction for a person they fund; while a deprivation of liberty referral is pending, the body it went to is told in the same way, including for a self-funder. The approver adds it to the restrictive practice register within 2 working days.

Care workers check equipment before each use as the visit plan and the Hoists, Slings and Lifting Equipment Procedure set out, and record each use as the visit plan directs, with any objection, distress or problem, in the daily visit notes. If the person objects, tries to climb over or out, gets a limb trapped, or the equipment is damaged or does not fit, the care worker does not use it, makes the person safe and phones the office before leaving; the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager (On-call Manager out of hours) decides the interim arrangement the same day, and the Care Coordinator tells the equipment's owner, usually the community equipment service, the same working day. Any other objection to a restriction is reported to the office the same day.

Where family or another agency carries out part of an agreed restriction, such as raising bed rails at night, the People involved part of the care plan records who does what, and the restriction is included in our assessment, screen and reviews.
Equipment and device restrictions also meet the conditions below.

rows: Bed rails and bed grab handles

A bed rail risk assessment by the health professional who prescribed or supplied them, as the Hoists, Slings and Lifting Equipment Procedure requires; alternatives such as a low bed or crash mat considered first (MHRA, Bed rails: management and safe use).
Lap belts and harnesses

Prescribed or assessed by an occupational therapist or physiotherapist for posture or safety. Staff never leave a person belted into a chair or wheelchair at the end of a visit unless the person can undo it themselves or the approved restriction records why it is needed and who will be with them.
Monitoring devices

Chosen under the Technology-Enabled Care and Telecare Policy; the visit plan says the alert is for checking on and supporting the person, never stopping them. One used to stop or bring back the person, or to monitor them for all or most of the day and night, is a significant restriction.
Locked storage and removed items

Only the item that creates the risk is secured; lockable medicines storage follows the Self-Administration of Medicines Procedure. A lock on a fridge or food cupboard is considered only on a health professional's advice for a specific risk, and the drinks and snacks the care plan sets are always left within reach (Nutrition and Hydration Policy).

blocks.p: Every review asks whether the restriction is still needed and whether it can be reduced, replaced or ended, and records the person's response to it since the last review.

blocks.p: A restriction that is no longer needed is ended at once, the visit plans updated, care workers told before their next visit and the register updated by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager within 2 working days. A restriction that the review shows is not working, or is causing harm, is suspended by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager the same day while an alternative is put in place.

sections.heading: Medicines used to manage distress or behaviour

blocks.p: Medicines can restrain. Whether a person has a medicine to calm or sedate them is the prescriber's decision, never ours, and we act only on their written direction, as the Consent, Mental Capacity and Declined Medicines Policy sets out.

bullets: Any medicine prescribed wholly or partly to manage distress, agitation or behaviour, regular or when required, is recorded as a restriction in the risk assessments and on the register, with its purpose and the person's consent or a best interests decision about our support with it; the Care Coordinator updates the deprivation of liberty screen the same working day it starts.

A when required medicine for distress has written guidance, under the When Required (PRN) Medicines Protocol, that lists the approaches to try first and the signs that a dose is needed. Care workers give it only as that guidance says, record on the eMAR what was tried and why the dose was given, and phone the office before leaving.

The Care Coordinator asks the prescriber for a review the same working day when such a dose is given at 3 or more visits in 7 days, or the person shows signs of over-sedation such as drowsiness, unsteadiness, falls or difficulty swallowing, which care workers phone to the office before leaving; a person who cannot be roused is a 999 call.

Supporting the national STOMP programme, the Care Coordinator asks the prescriber in writing at every scheduled care plan review whether each medicine used to manage behaviour is still needed, and records the answer.

blocks.p: Relatives, privately employed carers and other services sometimes restrict a person. Care workers phone the office before leaving the visit if anyone locks the person in, takes their keys or aids, restrains them, sedates them, or keeps visitors away. The safeguarding lead assesses the risk within 1 hour under the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure, and the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) updates the deprivation of liberty screen the same working day.

Where the person is restrained or locked in by others, strongly objects or tries to leave in a way that puts them at serious risk, the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager phones the commissioner the same day (out of hours, the On-call Manager phones the local authority emergency duty team) under the Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure. A person locked in alone is a fire risk, reported to the local authority the same day and referred by the Care Coordinator to the fire and rescue service the same working day under the Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy. The Care Coordinator discusses less restrictive alternatives with the family.

sections.heading: Emergency intervention and what happens afterwards

subsections.heading: When an emergency intervention is allowed

blocks.p: A care worker may act physically only to stop immediate serious harm to the person or someone else, when talking, giving space, removing the danger or leaving would not work in time. Examples are moving a person's hand away from a lit hob, or guiding a person back from the kerb as traffic approaches. The care worker uses the least force for the shortest time, stops as soon as the danger has passed, and never uses any practice listed in Practices we never use. Staff being grabbed or hit use only breakaway techniques or the least force needed to get away (Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy). Where the danger continues, they call 999.

steps: Stay with the person, speak calmly and reassure them. Check their breathing, colour, pain and any injury, and call 999 at once for difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse, a head injury or a suspected fracture. After calling 999, stay until help arrives or the office says you may leave.
Watch the person for the rest of the visit for pain, distress or any change, and record any injury on the CareFlow body map; never photograph it to gather evidence.
Phone the office, or the On-call Manager out of hours, before leaving and speak to a person. This is reported as unapproved restraint and a safeguarding concern.

Before the end of the shift, report in the CareFlow app, as an incident marked as a safeguarding concern, what happened before, during and after: the danger, what was tried first, exactly what was done, for how long, and the person's response, in their own words where possible.

blocks.p: An emergency intervention is never treated as a reason to plan restraint. Where the review finds that force was used when it was not necessary, or a prohibited practice was used, the Managing Allegations Against Staff Procedure and the Disciplinary Policy and Procedure apply.

blocks.p: Understanding distressed behaviour, positive behaviour support and breakaway training follow the Violence and Aggression Towards Staff Policy. Any external course we use that includes physical skills is certified against the Restraint Reduction Network Training Standards.

At every spot check where a restriction applies, the Field Care Supervisor observes it being used as recorded and asks the care worker which restrictions apply, what they must never do and what they would do if the person became distressed, and records the findings in the supervision and appraisal records. A shortfall means feedback the same day, retraining before the worker next applies the restriction and re-observation within 4 weeks. Staff acknowledge this policy in CareFlow by the deadline in the Induction and Care Certificate Procedure and within 14 days of each new major version.

blocks.p: Our targets are 100% of restrictions approved before use, 100% of reviews on time, no prohibited practice used, 100% of post-incident reviews within 10 working days, and a reduction each year in restrictions per person supported. Every shortfall goes in the service improvement plan within 5 working days with an owner and a deadline. Commissioners are given information about restrictions used for people they fund within 2 working days of a request.

This policy is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager, checked by the Nominated Individual and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy. It is reviewed sooner after a change in law or national guidance, a serious incident involving restraint, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows the arrangements are not working.
